Refs #939. This is the half of #939 that made it *invisible*, and it's separable from the delivery-semantics decision that issue still needs.

## The defect

When the update flow's terminal is `needs-human`, the converge has **delivered nothing** — the PR is open, parked, waiting for a person. But the runner labelled the PR and then **returned normally**. The executor's contract is `if (!result.ok)` → converge to `needs-human`, so a clean exit closed the work item **`outcome:done`**.

The specimen, from TLDR's own run last night:

| | |
|---|---|
| work item #268 | closed **`outcome:done`** at 00:14:23Z |
| PR #283 | open, labelled **`needs-human`**, "the converged tree FAILED its self-test" |

Same run, same moment. Every member's nightly update reported success like this for five days while the entire fleet sat frozen on one canon ref. The queue's signals were all green; nothing was.

The rehearsal path already exits non-zero on this exact terminal. Only the real path didn't.

## Why non-zero is right here

The house rule is "an expected, handled outcome exits clean; reserve non-zero for genuine breakage." A parked PR *is* the genuine breakage: the member has stopped converging, and nothing else in the system will say so. The label on the PR is not a signal anyone reads — five days of evidence.

## Verification

Seen to fail first: removing the `process.exitCode = 1` line fails the new test.

The test anchors on the terminal-dispatch block specifically, because the same `terminal.action === 'needs-human'` comparison appears twice earlier in the file on paths that already exit non-zero — anchoring naively passes against the wrong branch (which is exactly what my first draft did).

`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — **1899 pass, 0 fail.**

The unfreeze from #938 is confirmed working on a real member: TLDR's forced converge now returns terminal **`apply-stage`** (PR missingbulb/TLDR#290) instead of `needs-human`. Its self-test passes on the converged tree for the first time since 2026-08-12.

# DESIGN §5, §10). This is the repo's ONLY cron, and it replaces the slot
# scheduler's content at the same path when `taskScheduler.dispatch` is `"queue"`
# — same file, same hashed minute, different mechanism, so the one-cron rule and
# every reader that knows this workflow by name keep holding.
#
# A thin shim: all logic lives in the vendored engine, so this file changes
# rarely. The minute below is a placeholder; bootstrap and the wiring converge
# rewrite it to this repo's stable hashed minute in :10–:50, computed by
# `node .claudinite/shared/engine/scheduler/hash-minute.mjs <owner/repo>`.
#
# TWO JOBS, IN ORDER. The tick is pure label mechanics over the issue list —
# instantiate each task's standing item at its anchor, ready what is due, reclaim
# dead executor claims — and evaluates no precondition and collects no signal. The
# drain is an ordinary executor run: it picks up what the tick just created, which
# is what keeps the common case's latency at zero even with no `labeled` event
# delivered. Lost events are therefore never the only delivery — they are latency
# sugar, which is what retires the re-arm.
#
# `workflow_dispatch` is not a convenience: it is the never-wait-for-the-cron
# lever every forced run, migration and validation burst depends on. Its one
# input is how that lever reaches ACROSS repos: the fleet enforcer dispatches
# this workflow naming the tasks to run now, and this member wakes its own
# standing items with its own token (DESIGN §8). The alternative — the enforcer
# editing every member's issues directly — would widen the fleet PAT to issue
# writes on every repository, for a job the member can do for itself.
name: Claudinite scheduler

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '26 * * * *'
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      wake:
        description: 'Task ids to run now (`pack/task` or a bare task name, space-separated) — wakes each one’s standing item regardless of its anchor'
        required: false
        type: string

# One tick at a time, always. The tick's duplicate-standing-item self-heal is
# written assuming exactly this — it closes every open family item but the oldest,
# which is safe precisely because two ticks never run at once.
concurrency:
  group: claudinite-tick
